checks: For coordinatewise x ≤ y, every admissible threshold for y is admissible for x with a weakly smaller ratio. Scaling by a positive scalar bijects admissible thresholds, and the zero row has infimum zero.
The full-capture threshold max_j x_j is positive for every nonzero row and gives the stated upper bound. At the zero row the bound still holds by the separate zero-row computation.

The upper continuity bound uses exact translation of the law and compares each fixed admissible t before taking its infimum. It remains valid at atoms and does not require continuity of the distribution function in t.

At a nonzero boundary row, the minimum over its finitely many positive coordinates is positive. The comparison with (1−δ_n)x holds at zero entries by nonnegativity of the approaching rows. This proves the lower bound even when the capacity vanishes. At the zero row the max-coordinate bound proves continuity.

Each of the m columns lies in the simplex on the fixed number of rows. The objective is a finite continuous sum on a nonempty compact product, and the achieved row counts have a minimum in a finite set, including when all weights vanish.
Archived source f62fe2e83b180bf3 §1 contains the stated definition, two continuity bounds and weighted attainment. Its raw digest matches the frozen provenance.

overlap.comparison: This proves rowwise threshold attainment and local capacity regularity for strictly positive uniform-simplex rows. The present claim instead concerns attainment over a stochastic matrix, using capacity continuity up to every orthant boundary for arbitrary simplex laws.

readability: The distinction between attainment of the matrix maximum and attainment of the threshold infimum is clear. For instance the threshold infimum at x=0 need not be achieved.
review_method: Independent mathematical proof review of the frozen normalized candidate
summary: The capacity is continuous for every barycentric probability law, including atomic laws and rows with zero entries. Compactness yields an attained maximum for the fixed finite matrix problem.
